Introduction
The organisms of the United Nations System represented in Colombia have decided to coordinate their activities by means of a common framework for planning and action, which will allow them to act jointly and to increase our contribution to the development of the country and the attainment of peace.
This framework, described in the present document, defines joint objectives for the next five years, highlights the strategies which will organise joint action, points to the procedures conceived for the evaluation of processes and results, and also states the financial contributions foreseen for the period 2000-2002.
The planned focus arises from experience, —the need to broaden programs that some agencies of the System jointly launched some years ago— and from the decision to support all Colombian actors engaged in the search of peace. Actions foresee the joint co-operation of the System with the various builders of Colombia: the national, departmental and local governments of Colombia, the private sector and the labour unions, and many non-government organisms and local communities.
With the assertion of these new commitments, the United Nations System wishes to reassert its will to cooperate with the great goals the country has set out to reach. 
Justification
Colombia is going through one of the most difficult periods of its republican history.
As the National Development Plan states:
“Colombian society has structural problems such as inequity in the distribution of income, poverty and violence, which our political system has been unable to solve. This profound crisis has led us to the loss of collective interest in public matters, a weakening of the rule of law, and the proliferation of armed actions and of intimidation as a political method.
The model of social development prevailing in the country is not feasible. It is so because conditions of inequity and poverty have not been overcome. These, on the contrary, have persisted. This model has propitiated a type of social interaction based on exclusion, which refuses homes and persons the opportunity to fully accomplish their human potential, in a context of goods and services offered by development and technology. The ground of social exclusion in modern capitalist societies arises from the academic and professional qualifications needed to reach in the labour market the ever scarcer technical and professional positions (…).  It would seem that in our society, on the contrary, exclusion arises from the base, that is to say, from a limited access to education, health and nutrition, as well as from the informality of the labour market (…) this would mean that the sectors with lower incomes do not even reach the point where they can compete for these positions. It is a model in which economic growth and newly created opportunities not only are not shared equitably by all the population, but which also reproduces inequity through several mechanisms. A model of this kind is not and cannot be any longer viable and sustainable.” 
There are in Colombia extreme and generalised conditions of exclusion in the economic, social and political fields, which have generated a profound crisis manifested in the restrictions for peaceful coexistence, the spread of the armed conflict, the loss of the historical dynamics of the improvement of collective welfare, and the most serious economic imbalances of the last 70 years. Furthermore, the country suffers the sequels of the international activities of drug-traffic.  Since these critical elements interact and are mutually strengthened, it is necessary to confront them concurrently. 
Colombians are suffering the consequences of the crisis and are working to overcome them.  The great majority of the population has a solid desire for peace, expresses and mobilises itself in the search for a peaceful solution of the conflicts, makes real efforts to recover conditions for coexistence, growth and collective welfare, and decidedly rejects the activities of drug-traffic. 
In their common diagnostic of Colombia, the agencies of the United Nations System find that the main obstacle for the attainment of peace and welfare in the country, to reinforce economic growth and to reach reasonable conditions for development, is the absence of a culture of respect for the rights of human beings. The spread of violent actions, the deterioration of the social contract and exclusion are the three great underlying causes of the difficulty in fully enforcing human rights. To overcome despair and to promote attention to rights is fully viable through a firm commitment of both government and the whole of society. The undertaking of this primordial task would allow for the spread of new values of coexistence, for the capacity to build together, to attain high rates of growth and to create conditions of welfare for all. 
The United States System is willing to support Colombia in its efforts to attain peace, economic growth and human development, within a framework of promotion and protection of human rights. 
Colombians will be the ones to define the road to their destiny and to establish priorities. The United Nations System does not offer them predefined solutions, but its will to cooperate broadly and decidedly on the attainment of conditions for the universal exercise of human rights, and through this, on the sustainment of peace, the improvement of participative democracy, economic growth and the welfare of all without exclusions. 
Facing the country’s needs, the United Nations System has comparative experience and advantages to cooperate effectively and to contribute to great processes of change. These comparative advantages arise from the political neutrality of the System, its capacity to summon support and the lessons learned in the whole world during the last 50 years. 
Occasionally it is said that the System is not so useful because it does not contribute abundant funds to  additional financing. This appraisal is not correct. Firstly, because lack of financing is not the main obstacle to development and the System can provide other relevant, or more relevant, resources in order to facilitate social cohesion, political and institutional development and democratic legitimacy; secondly, because the System has the option to summon the financial support of the international community, thirdly, because the organisms of technical cooperation collaborate with the World Bank, which is one of the main instruments for the financing of development and is a member of the United Nations System.
Among the non financial advantages of the United Nations System, the following are pertinent to Colombia:
Mandate, orientation and experience regarding human rights. The main problem of the country, as has already been said, is the lack of an effective and universal exercise of human rights, and the absence of the guarantees required for the accomplishment of this exercise. The United Nations System has as its main focus, conferred by the international community, precisely the support for the achievement of the exercise of human rights. Under this mandate it has successfully participated in the improvement of the situation of rights in several countries.
Experience in the support of peace processes. In several countries, the System has played a decisive role in the negotiations for the suspension of internal armed conflicts. Simultaneously, it has great experience in the processes of construction of conditions for attaining and preserving peace, and in the mobilisation of support for the social, economic and political reconstruction of the affected nations. In various countries, the System has presently the role of external agent for the monitoring and promotion of compliance with the peace accords. 
The accumulated experience and positive results obtained in the country. The System has promoted and now supports some experiences of local and regional development, based on the mobilisation of public, private and communal agents, that have had great impact and can be considered models for other nations, such as the program “Desarrollo y Paz (Development and Peace) of the Magdalena Medio”, the “Municipios Saludables por la Paz” (Healthy Towns for Peace), the programs of alternative development in areas of coca under cultivation, the programs of assistance to displaced families, the programs of institutional and social development in several departments, and the support for scientific research on the social situation of the country, with emphasis on poverty and exclusion. 
The capacity to summon support, and mediation in the national context. As in other countries, it is possible that the main contribution of the United Nations is to bring about the construction of agreements centering on peace and the agreed upon contribution to the great national development goals; to support on this ground the formulation of public policies broadly arranged; and to facilitate the promotion and spread of a focus on rights that may contribute to the consolidation of social cohesion. 
The capacity to summon support, and mediation in the international context. In the actual context of globalisation, countries are increasingly interdependent; furthermore, some of the problems confronted by Colombia have roots or consequences of an international nature. For this reason, to overcome the several present problems and to find again the dynamics of accelerated growth Colombia requires international participation. But in the international context, the complexity of the many causes of the problems confronted by Colombia has given rise to simplistic interpretations in certain cases, or that do not facilitate solutions. The United Nations System has experience and legitimacy to make a greater international understanding of the situation in Colombia easier, and to obtain greater support of other countries for its processes of economic, political and social recuperation. 
Capacity to transfer experience and knowledge. Several nations have successfully confronted difficulties of development similar to those found in Colombia. The United Nations System, present in 170 countries, has the greatest disposable capacity to identify and transfer experience and knowledge, particularly in the areas of social development, territorial management, public policies, institutional development and human rights, that relatively have the weakest channels for international exchange. 
Capacity of adaptation to national conditions and flexibility. The United Nations System has the capacity to adapt itself to various contexts and the ability to look after unexpected circumstances. Experience has demonstrated that opportuness and adaptability usually have more impact than the amount or continuity of contributions. Flexibility is the ground for innovation, the condition to be able to enlist the best experts and an advantage in alliances with non-traditional organisations. 
The evaluation of its cooperation in Colombia done by the United Nations System shows that it has not made the maximum use of its comparative advantages. There has been dispersion of efforts and resources, because the demands of cooperation have been erratic and because the different agencies of the System present in the country have traditionally worked under a weak coordination. 
In the country as well as in the United Nations System there is the clear decision to improve the impact of cooperation in answer to the national needs and priorities. By the mandate of the nations of the world, the System has begun in its main headquarters and in several countries the cordination of the approaches, strategies and resources of the different agencies and existing funds.  In Colombia, the agencies of the System have already undertaken several joint activities, in which the experience and the specialisation of each one is combined to achieve a greater coordination and better results in their support.  
The process toward integration began in Colombia with the drawing up of a shared diagnostic on the situation of the country. The diagnostic, contained in the document, “Colombia: Discovering the Rights to Build the Nation”, allowed the agencies to adopt a common position on the problems and challenges facing the country, and it encouraged the pledge to contribute to the solution of the first and to make the success in the overcoming of the latter easier. The agencies of the System also carried out a collective analysis of the National Development Plan and of the Strategy of Diplomacy for Peace, both prepared by the national government, and that the United Nations System considers as a call for international cooperation in the prioritary efforts of the country.
In the following section you will find a summary of the national policies, based on which the United Nations System can boost in Colombia its comparative advantages, concentrating in some areas of cooperation specially relevant for the country and consistent with the mandate given to the System by the international community. 
The main areas of cooperation presented in the subsequent sections, are precisely those in which there is a greater convergence of the mandatory norms given by the international community, the joint diagnostic drawn up by the United Nations System, and the national development policies of the Colombian government. 
2.  National Cooperation Aims and Objectives
The cooperation of the United Nations System in any given country is based on two basic orientations: the public development policies of the country and the mandate of the international community received by the System.
In Colombia, the United Nations System gives its support to the principles of the Constitution and shares the yearning of Colombians for cohesion, growth and welfare, presented in the National Development Plan accorded by law. 
The cooperation of the United Nations System will therefore be committed to the results of the change, growth and welfare set out by the country. This perspective of an effective compromise with the national objectives has been named, “program focus”, and it implies that cooperation will be successful if and only the national program in which it is in line achieves its foreseen objectives. “Program focus” also implies that the United Nations System does not have its own programs, but that it cooperates with the programs being executed by the government and other social agents. 
The national orientations and the cooperative aims of the United Nations System are examined next.
The great orientations of national development and, consequently, of the cooperation of the United Nations System, are defined by the Constitution of 1991, by the National Development Plan, by the strategy of Diplomacy for Peace, which is part of the same, and by strategic sectorial policies.  
a.  The National Constitution
The Constitution of the Republic of Colombia was approved in 1991, as a result of a broadly participative democratic exercise. 
The basic framework of the Constitution is its charter of rights, established in Chapter II, immediately after the fundamental principles. The fundamental rights —social, economic, cultural, collective and environmental— are broadly and clearly recognised along its 84 articles. Furthermore, conditions for the protection and the application of rights are established, as well as the duties and obligations derived from them. 
The Colombian Constitution expresses the collective will and must become an effective guide of action for the state and the citizens. The cooperation of the United Nations System will be aimed at contributing directly to the full compliance with the constitutional rules with regard to human rights. 
b. The National Development Plan
The development goals for the period 1998-2002 have been established by the Colombian Government in the National Development Plan, called “Change for the Building of Peace”.
The National Development Plan aims at the attainment of peace. This is understood as the overcoming of social conflict, manifested mainly in violence and poverty. 
Two basic causes of violence and poverty are identified: the social inability to settle tensions —which has given rise to a fragmented society and a very low social cohesion— and the presence of very serious macroeconomic imbalances originated in the nineties and is related to the sharp fall of economic growth —which in 1999 reached negative rates for the first time in 70 years—, the fiscal deficit and the deficit in the current account of the balance of payment.
In keeping with its diagnostic, the National Development Plan aims mainly at the attainment of peace through the construction of a road to economic growth with social cohesion. 
From this general objective four specific goals emerge, all of them aiming at overcoming poverty, social justice, the development of a culture of peace and respect for human rights:
To promote the production of wealth and a significant cutback in unemployment, in order to ensure its equitable distribution, the elimination of poverty and an adequate exploitation of the environment.
To facilitate the social and economic promotion of the population and equality in social opportunities, with emphasis in those under conditions of particular vulnerability, on account of their socio-economic, cultural, ethnic, territorial, religious or gender characteristics.
To contribute to the creation of a culture of peace based on the daily exercise of coexistence in a climate of solidarity, tolerance and respect for human rights as a basis for national reconciliation.
To improve efficiency and equity in the allocation of public resources, taking into account criteria of regional and gender income and distribution.
The plan aims at the achievement of these objectives by means of four main strategies:
Strengthening of participative democracy, through a process of political reform that ensures a return to governance (democratic institutions conducive to peace,  and a technical and transparent work by the Congress) and a new restructuring of the state based on the modernisation of public administration and the achievement of a greater degree of decentralisation. 
A restructuring of the social fabric, through compromises of the state and society for the reduction of exclusion, the eradication of poverty and the attainment of a new ethics of social coexistence, by means of two central policies: the improvement of human capital (provision of capacities and opportunities), and the construction of social capital (trust and participation). In this way, the reconstruction of the social fabric is based on the total coverage of education and health, alimentary security, full assistance to minors, the improvement of intrafamily relations and equality of genders. 
Peace for Development and Development for Peace, through negotiation with the armed groups and their reinsertion in civil life; at the same time, the reduction of inequality and poverty to attain uniformity of opportunities in the areas of conflict. Agricultural and livestock development, the strengthening of civil society in areas most affected by conflict and violence, the restructuring of the infrastructure, the re-institutionalisation of justice and the restoration of security, are planned within this strategy. 
Exports as a promoter of economic growth, to manage the internalisation of the economy so as to redirect the productive sector to achieve a new dynamics, create jobs, and facilitate a successful incorporation into the world economy. This strategy implies the overcoming of the rigid structures that prevent an increase in productivity, to improve the exporting infrastructure and to take advantage of the tourist industry  potential of the country.
c. Diplomacy for peace
The national government aims at a specific strategy for its foreign policy, which it has called “Diplomacy for Peace”, also included in the National Development Plan.
Diplomacy for Peace arises from the recognition that the process of globalisation has brought together the foreign and domestic policies in a decisive and increasing manner, and that in the road to peace the help of the international community is an indispensable complement of internal efforts. Its objective is then to obtain the support and collaboration of the industrialised nations and of the international organisms, in order to begin the economic and social redemption of the regions most affected by the armed conflict, and to attain the economic and commercial conditions necessary to reach levels of growth capable of supporting and sustaining the peace process. 
Diplomacy for Peace includes, among others, the following policies:
Foreign policy regarding Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law (complementary to the internal policies in the same areas).  Its focal point is the strengthening of the multilateral and intergovernmental focus in matters of human rights, through:  i) the design and monitoring of an integral policy of human rights and international humanitarian law, in coordination with the responsible national entities and following the recommendations of the proper organisms of the United Nations and of the Interamerican System; ii) to deal with the international organisms in an adequate and opportune manner, in individual cases and in reports of a general character; and iii) to improve communications with government and non government international organisms specialising in human rights and international humanitarian law. 
Policies regarding the world problem of illicit drugs. The focal point of Colombian policy in this field is the progressive and systematic reduction of the causes and manifestations of the drug problem, in a manner related to policies on peace. Actions aim at achieving alternative development in areas with illicit crops, with feasible options for the peasant population that lives from them, and to manage a foreign policy that allows for the recognition of the principles of shared responsibility, integrality and equilibrium, and capable of improving cooperation in this field. These objectives imply the following foreign policy actions: i) to commit the international community to modalities of cooperation tending to balance political, social, economic and environmental costs of the fight against drugs, ii) to search for greater technical and financial international cooperation for programs of alternative development, iii) to achieve in the countries of origin greater control of the production and marketing of chemical precursors and substances used in the manufacture of illicit drugs; iv) to strengthen the organisations and legal systems fighting against and punishing crimes in the field of illicit drugs; v) to give impetus to measures for the prevention and control of money laundering in the world financial market; and vii) to raise awareness in the international community of the efforts and costs that the problem of drugs implies for Colombia, relying in this matter on political, economic and social studies measuring the  real impact of the problem in the country. 
The policy for the international control of the arms trade aims at a considerable reduction of the supply, distribution and use of firearms, through the following actions: i) legal approval of the convention on the use, production, storage and transfer of anti-personal mines; ii) control of the proliferation and illicit trade of small arms through participation in the United Nations Group of Government Experts on Small Arms; iii) control of the illicit arms trade in conformity with the Interamerican Convention against the illicit manufacture and traffic of firearms, explosives, munitions and related materials; iv) continue the promotion in the United Nations of an International Conference on the illicit arms trade, as requested by Colombia; v) to reach agreements with neighbouring countries to fight against the illicit traffic of arms across borders; and vi) prohibition of the production, storage and transfer of chemical arms. 
The strategy of Diplomacy for Peace has as one of its focal points the Plan Colombia, conceived by the Government as a set of demands presented to the international community in favour of peace and the strengthening of the state.
The United Nations System supports initiatives such as Diplomacy for Peace which do not lead to an escalation of the armed conflict, and in particular aiming at:
alternative development in areas of illicit  crops exploited by poor peasants;
reforming the law through the establishment of an impartial, equitable and effective legal system (reduction of impunity, better access of the population to the law, increment of the promptness and effectiveness of judicial proceedings, establishment of an effective accusatory system, and the fight against corruption);
democratisation and social development through an increment in the presence and legitimacy of the state in the regional context (development of rural areas, promotion of respect and protection of human rights, assistance to victims of violence, with particular  emphasis on the promotion of the rights of displaced persons and assistance to their needs);
supporting the peace process through the demobilisation of armed actors and their reinsertion in civil society (establishment of a national consensus regarding peace, peace agreement with the insurgents based on the principles of territorial integrity, democracy and respect for human rights;
economic reactivation in order  to recover basic economic equilibrium and the dynamics of the Colombian economy (adequate integration into the global context, increment of the productivity of the industrial sector and modernisation of the exporting infrastructure; and
an international control of the arms traffic.

As asserted above, the objectives of the cooperation in Colombian development of the United Nations System arise from the goals and strategies of national development which have just been presented, as well as from the mandate received by the System from the international community and the comparative advantages of its agencies facing the challenge of development. 
The general objective of its cooperation is to contribute to the construction of a coexisting society, sustainable economic growth, and collective equity and welfare, through the strengthening of the exercise of human rights.
 This objective implies that the cooperation of the System will aim at contributing directly to the attainment of the great goals foreseen in the National Development Plan, which are defined as economic growth with social cohesion, and specify four objectives: i) equitable distribution and elimination of poverty; ii) social and economic promotion of the population and of equality of social opportunities; iii) creation of a culture of peace; and iv) efficiency and equity in the allocation of resources.
Why through the exercise of human rights?
Because they are a necessary and unavoidable condition for the attainment of peace and to create the conditions for economic growth and social welfare needed by the country. 
Colombia is a nation confronting very great challenges for the promotion, protection and application of human rights. As stated by the National Development Plan, the main challenges facing the nation have to do with structural problems such as inequity in the distribution of incomes, poverty and violence, which the political system has been incapable to solve and which have led to the worsening of relations among persons, to break norms, to the extensive use of armed practices and the resort to intimidation as a political method. 
The already mentioned problems and the high degree of violence existing in Colombia  have led to a particular perception of rights, in so far as the majority of Colombians identify human rights with the most serious conducts product of violence. For many Colombians, persons and organisations, human rights are exclusively linked to violations of International Humanitarian Law, such as massacres, torture, attacks against civilians and forced displacement. 
Then, the Colombian view of human rights has been restricted to a small field which does not sufficiently takes into account the relations between the state and the citizens, and between the individual and the community; and it also disregards the indivisibility of civil and political, economic, social and cultural rights. 
The biased perception mentioned above does not take into account two important aspects in the Colombian case: i) peace, security and human development are comprehensively bound and are reciprocally reinforced. Exclusion, poverty and inequality undermine human rights, and increase social unease and violence. To promote and protect all of those rights is to prevent conflicts that have their roots in social injustice, poverty, discrimination and exclusion. Ii) The exercise of human rights empowers individuals and communities, creates the necessary conditions for economic growth and is the essential foundation of collective welfare. 
Several sectors of the government and society are beginning to understand that human rights refer to the range of minimal conditions necessary for individuals to enjoy security and to be able to have an acceptable life, make the welfare of others easier and contribute to an economic growth that can reinforce and broaden collective welfare.  The right to preserve life without putting it in danger or run the risk of losing directly by others, or by their omission or negligence. Civil and political rights as the option to exercise liberty of election or association in various contexts, to act under conditions and rules equal for all, and to be protected by an independent, opportune and egalitarian system of justice. Economic and social rights, such as having a minimal income to subsist, feed oneself, have access to basic education, count on effective health services, have a place to live and liberty to move in a healthy environment. The exercise of these rights allows persons to live with dignity, to be included in the economic and political life of the country and to contribute to its growth, to be able to expand their businesses and to consider legitimate the institutions that make possible and protect the universal application of these rights. 
As the National Development Plan acknowledges, the main objective of the nation is Human Development, which is no other than the full adherence to human rights, exercised, respected and enjoyed by all. 
Human rights are the foundation of peace and coexistence, of social cohesion and of a sustainable economic growth. For social cohesion there are four basic reasons: i) because they imply universality, so as to overcome exclusion and inequity in any form; ii) because to exercise a right implies duties for the same person who exercises them, as well as respect for the collective rights (the right to education, for example, calls for the fulfilment of educational responsibilities); iii) because a sustainable rule of law means the full participation of all citizens in the process of decision taking on matters affecting their lives and the lives of their children; and iv) because in themselves they imply an ethics of relationships among citizens. Human rights are also the foundation of economic growth, because they express the minimal conditions necessary for the development of human capital (opportunities) and also of social capital (the rule of law, equality facing the market, minimisation of costs of social transaction and cohesion).
The Rule of Law is, essentially, a constitutional framework that facilitates, promotes, oversees and warrants the validity of the rights of all human beings, thus making growth and welfare easier. 
Under this perspective, the general objective of the support given in Colombia by the United Nations System is then to work together and cooperate with all government and society’s bodies for the securing of human rights, aiming at the attainment of the great goals and compromises Colombia has set out to achieve. 
State, Society and Human Rights
Colombia, as a full Member State of the United Nations, has adopted the United Nations Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and all international pacts regarding Civil and Political Rights, as well as Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. In this sense, the Colombian State has accepted the unavoidable obligation to enforce all the human rights of all persons. Appendix II contains a list of all the international compromises of Colombia on the matter of human rights. 
The role of individuals and their organisations must also be underlined: each individual has duties with regard to others and to the community to which he or she belongs. Each individual is under the obligation to promote and respect human rights as acknowledged in international pacts.
The state as well as the citizens play important roles in the effective enforcement of rights. Both must work towards the creation of conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations contained in the treaties be effective, promoting in this manner the welfare of all persons on the base of their active participation in the life of society and in the just distribution of the benefits resulting from it. 
However, the Colombian state has the main responsibility of being the main warrantor of human rights, through its full respect in all the activities of the authorities, the guarantee of its exercise by all citizens, and the exercise of its duties of overseeing and promoting within its competence; and through the spread and promotion of a culture of rights in the country.
The specific objectives of the United Nations System cooperation directly concern the goals set by the National Development Plan and Diplomacy for Peace. These objectives concern the context of human rights (right to life, civil and political, economic, social and cultural rights), which are the basic mandate of the United Nations System and identify the areas in which it cooperates with the national government and other agents of development in the country. 
In the context of human right to life, to make progress regarding the protection of human life and personal integrity
This objective includes three great components:
Reduction of deaths caused by violence and in particular those caused by:
the armed conflict
every day violence
negligence, particularly in traffic and workplace accidents
Substantial progress regarding the respect for International Humanitarian Law, specially on the matter of:
suspension of executions
suspension of massacres
suspension of the storming of towns
suspension of the arbitrary deprivation of liberty, extortive or political kidnappings, and the forced disappearance of persons
prevention of the causes of forced displacement, and of the use of this tactic as a strategy of war
stopping the participation of minors in the armed conflict
These objectives related to International Humanitarian Law are valid even if the armed conflict continues, and progress in regard to them will surely be a substantial step towards a negotiated solution of the said conflict. 
An important  reduction of aggression against women and children of both sexes, specially through:
the reduction in sexual violence
the reduction of intrafamily violence
the reduction of violence in schools
In the context of civil and political rights, strengthening of a participative, democratic and equitable state under the rule of law
This second objective includes four areas:
Development of a culture of legality based on:
spread of legality for the establishment of single, universal and stable proceedings
reduction of informality for the establishment of rules accessible to all citizens; incentives and conditions for demands
Universal access and improvement of the efficiency and effectiveness in the administration of justice as to:
the spread of opportunities of access to traditional and non judicial mechanisms for the administration of justice
-full respect for proper legal action, including promptness and efficiency in legal proceedings
-the establishment of a prison system respectful to the rights of the accused and convicted
-securing of the right to redress
Improvement of the openness of public administration, specially in regard to:
a reduction of corruption
a reduction in abuses of power and authority
the establishment of more and better mechanisms of giving accounts and citizen supervision
Improvement in the establishment of a democratic and effective local administration particularly in regard to:
a greater political, administrative and fiscal decentralisation
an increment of citizen participation in the process of choosing, planning and  controlling local administrations
the development of a culture of giving accounts and impact evaluation
In the context of economic, social and cultural rights, universality and equity in gender access to basic services and the benefits of development
This objective includes:
Universal access to an income, through:
the promotion of better conditions for productive investment and economic growth   
the reduction of unemployment
international competitiveness and technological innovation
the reduction of informal work
supplying small urban and rural producers better channels of access to productive resources
alternative agricultural and livestock development
the improvement of training for work
regional development
Universal access and improvement of the quality of education, through:
an increment in the coverage of institutional pre-school education, specially to support of families without the means to pay for it
attainment of full coverage of the first five years of basic education
education for democracy, coexistence and respect for human rights since school
Universal access and improvement of the quality of prevention and health assistance, through:
full access to public health
universal affiliation to the Health Social Security System, making thus possible the access of everyone to the Compulsory Health Plan
prevention of HIV/AIDS, and integral assistance to all persons affected or carriers, and promotion of respect for their rights
Universal access to alimentary security, specially through:
access of all the population to the minimal nutritional requirements, including micro-nutrients
the attainment of sustainable conditions of agricultural and fishing development
Universal access to sustainable human settlement, through:
the improvement of conditions of access to housing (with intervention on demand or supply)
massive application of minimal standards of healthy and safe housing
an increment in the coverage of drinking water at homes
Universal access a healthy environment through:
increase in the coverage of systems of excrement disposal and water services
adequate disposal of solid wastes
protection of water sources and bodies
control of environmental pollution
To attain an integral and sustainable economic development for society to be able to adequately finance universal access to the aforementioned rights.
The specified objectives are, without any doubt, ambitious, but they concern aspects that national society must inexcusably take into account in order to achieve conditions of sustainable human development. The United Nations System aims at contributing to these objectives through the strategies studied next. 
3.  Strategies and Expected Results of Cooperation
The search for the objectives identified in the previous section is achieved through specific operative strategies. With each strategy the aim will be to bring about the attainment of the established objectives.
The strategies of the cooperation in Colombia of the United Nations System have been agreed upon in accordance to the lessons of experience and comparative advantages of the System applicable in Colombia.
There are specific strategies for three contexts: local, national and international. In each case the foreseen results are laid out. 
The basic strategy in the local area is to promote and oversee integrated programs of social cohesion, institutional development and economic growth, with the purpose of attaining conditions of sustainable peace and development, the participation of all actors in territorial life, and national scope, so that the models with the most impact can be used in any other part of the country.
Under this strategy, actions will be undertaken following three models: i) humanitarian assistance and reinsertion of displaced persons; ii) alternative agricultural and livestock development; and iii) development and peace in regional and municipal areas. The first model aims at taking care of the immediate needs of the victims of the present conflicts, while the other two are prototypes for the recovery of social cohesion together with the construction of a sustainable and equitable productive performance. Under the three models, the participation of the beneficiaries in the formulation, execution and evaluation of the initiatives of cooperation of the System of the United Nations will be decidedly fostered. 
The characteristics of the models of joint cooperation in the local area are the following:
Response to the situation of forced displacement: prevention, emergency humanitarian assistance and socio-economic reinsertion.
The phenomenon of forced displacement as a consequence of violence is one of the main manifestations of the humanitarian crisis with its accompanying violations of human rights and of International Humanitarian Law (IHL). This situation, present in all of the Colombian territory, continues without adequate response, in a context of degradation of the armed conflict with the intensification of violence and a relative standstill of the process of negotiation.
To make more effective and coherent the assistance to displaced persons by the United Nations System (UNS), a Thematic Group on Displacement  (GTD) was created. This is presently allowing the UNS to use a platform for common focus and action, which favours the development of joint work with various state institutions and non government organisations in the areas of greatest concern. 
The agencies of the UNS, in compliance with its mandate, engage in activities of prevention, protection and assistance to displaced persons.  On the other hand, the agencies coordinate their work in the following areas of intervention: emergency humanitarian assistance, information systems, reinsertion and reintegration, and institutional strengthening. 
On the matters of prevention of displacement and protection of the rights of the displaced persons, one of the most remarkable initiatives is the establishment of a System of Early Alerts. Emergency humanitarian assistance consists above all in the promotion of actions of alimentary security, health, drinking water and basic sanitation. The UNS is also promoting the improvement of the systems of information on displacement, through its support to a series of government and non-government organisations with experience and/or mandate in the matter.
The agencies of the UNS concentrate the greatest part of their intervention on the programs of reinsertion and reintegration. The main points of work are the following: a) integral improvement of human settlements; b) assistance and access to basic health services and basic infrastructure, and c) strengthening of the social organisation working on productive projects and their articulation in productive chains. The strengthening of the state entities in charge of forced displacement is done under a double perspective: on the one hand, collaboration is offered to the national entities responsible for the design and execution of public policies for integral assistance to the displaced population; on the other, support is given to the institutional public capacity of management and cooperation, in the central level as well as in the local level (Network of Social Solidarity, Departments, Townships).
The definition of the expected results in matter of prevention, protection, assistance and reinsertion will be done, once the precise indicators of displacement in the country are established.  These indicators will be useful to find out the progress or setbacks in the matter of displacement, for the state to give account and for the overseeing by the public.
Subregional programs of development and peace
The program Development and Peace, undertaken in the Magdalena Medio with actions in 17 municipalities, is headed by the inhabitants of the region themselves, driven by a team of promotion and the support of the United Nations System, municipal administrations and several government, non government and communal organisations. The Program has already shown very promising results as a model for the building up of coexistence and a sustainable economy in areas of great polarisation, characterised by heterogeneous social actors who normally tend to implant their own particular hegemony to the exclusion of others. Actions will continue being carried out in the Magdalena Medio, with contributions of the UNDP, the World Bank, WFP, FAO, UNFPA and other organisms of the System, and will be extended to 5 other areas, making use of the program already underway.
A similar strategy is promoted by UNICEF in nearly 80 municipalities of the departments of Nariño, Cauca, Chocó, Córdoba, Putumayo, Caquetá, Meta and Amazonas, in the Urabá in Antioquia and in the town of Bello. 
The expected result for the period 2000-2001 is the mobilisation of 2 million inhabitants of various areas of conflict aiming at the recovery of their capacity of peaceful coexistence, the improvement of their conditions of social development, a productive reactivation and the attainment of conditions of governance.
Alternative agricultural and livestock development
Under the coordination of the UNDCP, several organisms of the United Nations System have made progress in the field of  alternative agricultural and livestock development, aiming at the substitution of illicit plantings and at the support for the productive development of very poor peasant communities. The strategy of substitution of illicit crops includes the promotion of legal crops, and facilities for the marketing of new agricultural products, and the socio-economic development of the affected areas. 
To initiate alternative production in 10% of the area with illicit crops is the result foreseen for the period 2000-2001.
Support for municipalities
Several agencies of the United Nations System actively cooperate with the integral development of municipalities. 
Current actions are guided by various strategies fostered by some agencies of the System, such as “Municipalities for Peace” by the WHO/PAHO, “Municipalities friendly to children” by UNICEF and “Local reconciliation and coexistence” by the UNDP. Use has also been made of the experience and contributions of WFP, FAO and UNFPA. These strategies and methodologies, actually in the process of reintegration, aim at the strengthening of the local social pact by means of the mutual action of the municipal authorities and the different levels of local society, including those groups traditionally included. Citizens participate actively in the definition of municipal plans of management and development in key areas, trying to make them equitable and sustainable. In this way steps are taken toward the building of a local, authentic participative democracy, and toward attaining more efficiency in management, with a positive impact on the reduction of socio-economic inequality, local economic growth, a lowering of drug abuse, fewer violent deaths, an improvement in citizen welfare, job creation and the provision of health, education, alimentary security, drinking water and basic sanitation. Progress is actually being made through several initiatives to establish networks of horizontal cooperation and exchange of opinions between the participating municipalities. 
The System has set out to make progress in the coordination of current experiences and in the joint reinforcement of the different participating agencies’ capacity of support, with the aim of achieving a greater cohesion in cooperation, broadening the coverage of the municipalities involved and facilitating the establishment of networks of horizontal cooperation and exchange of experiences. 
The organisms of the United Nations System will arrange and unify efforts in order to facilitate integral support —in 100 municipalities— for the municipal administrations, local communities and various government and non government organisations, in activities aiming at: i) the promotion of coexistence and social cohesion; ii) local institutional development; iii) the universalization of basic local services; iv) the establishment of mechanisms of justice on a local level; v) the fostering of production; and vii) the provision of information for citizens’ control and overseeing. 
The basic strategies in the national context are three: i) to facilitate the overseeing of human development and the process of change for peace and social cohesion; ii) support for the design and implementation of national public policies aiming at the assistance to basic rights; and iii) to facilitate the peace agreements.
Human Development Observatory with a Focus on Rights
The country counts with good overseeing of the economy by the state, through opportune, reliable and public indicators, aiming at facilitating the decisions of the economic agents. This strategy aims at supporting the establishment of a parallel system for the permanent and public monitoring of the social situation, through indicators of human and institutional development and of access to public services. 
Its antecedent is a report on Human Development drawn up during the last two years, which will be expanded with a statistical monthly, quarterly and annual report. Its sources will be the specialised public entities with available information, and improving in certain cases the methods of register or the coverage of surveys. 
The expected result is a “Human Development Observatory with a Focus on Rights”, capable of promoting a better overseeing by citizens of progress in development and in the accountability of all actors of development —concerning results—, including the community itself. On this base, institutions will be more transparent and thus more legitimate. 
The “Human Development Observatory with a Focus on Rights”, with a national character, will be duplicated in several regions of the country, with the participation of government and non government agents, aiming at promoting accountability and the overseeing by citizens in the regional context. 
The Observatory will be the core instrument for the overseeing of actions related to the cooperation of the United Nations System, as will be examined in the next chapter.
Appendix 1 includes the basic variables to be considered by the Observatory.
Human Rights
The United Nations System will draw up periodic reports on the exercise of human rights in Colombia and, therefore, on the minimal conditions for the social, economic and political welfare of its inhabitants. To this end it counts on the specific mandate of the Human Rights Commission of the United Nations System. These reports will be drawn up by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights of the United Nations, with the collaboration of all the specialised agencies. On the other hand, the Observatory described in the previous paragraphs, will be useful to the international community as a reliable instrument for monitoring the progress being made by the country on the matter of Human Development with a focus on rights. 
Support for national politics aiming at the assistance to basic rights
By request of the National Government, the United Nations System will cooperate in the design and execution of national programs aiming at facilitating the exercise of human rights in the areas and aspects identified in the specific objectives mentioned in the previous section. 
Cooperation will preferably be offered in aspects in which the System has comparative advantages: access to international experience, capacity to summon the support of different actors for common objectives and programs, capacity for mediating in conflicting matters or relations, capacity for social mobilisation and to call for international support.
The expected result is the design of public policies on matters of basic service, technically solid and politically more consensual and legitimate.
Stress must be put on the orienting role that the National Plan of Action on Human Rights and the National Plan for education in the area of human rights will play. Those plans are being developed by the System jointly with the Office of the Vice-president and the Ministry of Education respectively.
Facilitation of the peace agreements
The peace agreements to resolve internal conflicts are hindered by mistrust between the parties or by suspicions of partiality that may be aroused by the mediators. For this reason, internal peace agreements en quite different nations have usually required external and impartial facilitators.
The United Nations System puts itself at the disposal of Colombia as a facilitator of the peace agreements, in view of its experience in this aspect of peace negotiations. This role, which would be accepted on the request of both parties, would include the search —together with all areas of society— for a strategic agreement on a possible future and on the compromises of each party to attain it, so that the peace agreements will be effective commitments of change and development for the whole society.
The strategy in the international context is to keep the international community informed on the situation of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law in Colombia, to promote, to stimulate the support of the international community for the peace efforts and the human development of the country, and to coordinate actions with other multilateral, bilateral and non government cooperators, for the benefit of the country.
This strategy is coordinated around two sets of actions: Diplomacy for Peace and the search of a better international understanding of the situation in Colombia. 
Diplomacy for Peace
The United Nations System will cooperate with the program Diplomacy for Peace in Colombia, seeking effective political, commercial and financial support for the Colombian efforts to attain peace and the full exercise of human rights, under the strategy of “Peace and Development”, put forward by the Secretary General as a fundamental pillar of the cooperation of the System. 
To this end, the Secretary General has named a Special Envoy who will coordinate the actions of the System in support to Diplomacy for Peace and will draw up recommendations to facilitate the securing of cooperation and support by other countries. This Special Envoy will count on the permanent support of all the agencies of the System acting in Colombia. The System of Resident Coordination will make efforts to balance the activities of cooperation within the country with the activities of  promotion, spread and mobilisation, backing Colombia in the international context. 
The expected result of this strategy will be the securing of the political and economic cooperation foreseen in Diplomacy for Peace, save in aspects that could affect the peace agreements or lead to an intensification of war. 
b. Spread and monitoring of the international recommendations
Colombia is signatory of most of the international treaties on human rights, in the world as well as the regional context. It also participates in international conferences related to the promotion of specific subjects. In this sense, the specialised agencies of the United Nations System advise and cooperate with the Colombian state in order that it fulfil the recommendations arising from those instruments and conferences. 
The expected result of this strategy is a better understanding of international rules, and actions to overcome the problems actually confronted by the country. This makes possible that the international community have a better knowledge of the situation of Colombia, which is an essential requirement for the securing of the support and solidarity that the country needs in its search of better conditions for peace, social cohesion and development. 
To make progress in the foreseen direction, the System has taken the following steps:
Appointment of the Special Envoy of the General Secretary of the United Nations for the International Assistance to Colombia, who performs his duties with the direct support of the Secretary General and of all the agencies of the System represented in Colombia.
The establishment of four interagency groups, who have begun to refine and coordinate the strategies put forward in this framework of cooperation (except in so far as the support to peace negotiations, not requested by the parties. These groups are:
Human rights, under the coordination of the UNHCHR, and aiming at activities in  the matter of monitoring the situation of human rights, it supports the drawing up of national policies in this field, cooperates with the international spread of the situation in Colombia and supports the other groups in educational activities on human rights and in the setting up of mechanisms of early alert;
Integral assistance to displaced persons, coordinated by the UNHCR, it is in charge of coordinating the interagency activities of support in this field, and of also giving support to the laying down of policies in the national context;
Alternative development, coordinated by the UNDCP, it facilitates harmonization and cooperation in the local as well as in the national level; and
Development and local and regional reconciliation, coordinated by the UNDP, it aims at orienting the activities of the strategies of Support for the Municipalities in the local context and of Development and Peace in the regional context, as well as at the laying down of policies pertinent to these fields.

5. Monitoring and evaluation
Two essential characteristics of the joint actions to be undertaken by the United Nations System within the present framework for its cooperation with the development of Colombia, are accountability and a sense of collective learning. Both characteristics require strict parameters of monitoring and evaluation.
The cooperation of the United Nations System in Colombia has as its only objective progress in human development and, thus, the exercise of human rights. That is, the effective result of cooperation is related to the rates of deaths on account of violence, indicators of access to the administration of justice, performance of the judicial system, indicators of corruption, income per capita, rates of absence from school, of access to health services, of the nutritional and housing situation, separated by sex, age groups and geographical location, as the case may be. 
With its “Program Focus”, the United Nations System commits itself with the results of the programs in which it takes part, and participates in the foreseen objectives to be attained by the actions of the involved national and international agents. As a consequence, the results obtained are a measure of actions under way. Because of this, it is indispensable to lay the foundations and mechanisms of evaluation for each of the programs being implemented.
Under these parameters, the evaluation of the results of the programs implies restrictions and difficulties, which must be carefully studied. The restrictions on the exercise of human rights are multiple and they set up a complex network of relations mutually reinforced. Looking at this fact, it is not possible to pretend that short term actions will produce drastic changes in the rates of violence or in social behaviour, even though they involve the efforts of very different national and international agents. 
Therefore, the evaluation of results does not expect substantial changes in the indicators or in behaviour, but must be sufficiently sensible to be able to detect specific modifications that may produce new dynamics, which gradually may lead to encourage the exercise of human rights and to stop the circuits that block them (such as violence, the falling apart of institutions, or obstacles found by the poorer to gain access to social services).
The evaluation of results will then focus on the identification of changes related to Human Development, in the national as well as the local contexts, by means of adequate indicators to that effect. 
The challenge is then to count on a set of indicators that can perform the operations described above and stimulate the social analysis and monitoring of its progress. This is precisely the function of the Human Development Observatory, mentioned in the section 3.2.a, and of the indicators specified in Appendix 1. 
A fundamental purpose is to manage that evaluation will be in itself an activity producer of changes in the attitudes, perceptions and behaviour of the citizens. With this objective in mind, it will be understood that evaluation is the accountability due to the participating communities and to the whole country. The aim will be then to make public the indicators of Human Development, for society to be the supervisor of the actions and that their attainments be a factor of hope and an invitation to a change of the citizens’ attitudes and behaviour, and to a tendency toward new initiatives. For this reason, the indicators, besides being broadly spread, will be accompanied by monographs on successful experiences and systematic procedures for the exchange of experiences. 
Most of the strategies set out in the previous section have a sense of learning: i) in the local context: the aim is to consolidate effective models and the reinsertion of the displaced persons, in order to create social processes of social cohesion and to optimise efforts in alternative development; ii) in the national context: the development of public policy with high impact on universality; and iii) in the international context: finding the best approach to the international community and obtaining its cooperation and support.
The monitoring and evaluation of the processes will be considered as an instrument of collective learning drawn from experience. Its objective is to get acquainted with the efficiency and efficacy of the actions underway, with the proposed objectives in mind. The systematisation of experiences assumes then an essential role as an instrument of learning. 
The monitoring and evaluation of the processes have certain special features according to the context in which the cooperation is done, as it is next described in detail:
a. In the local context
The monitoring an evaluation of local actions (assistance to displaced persons, development and peace, alternative development, municipal development) will have two objectives: i) to facilitate the social appropriation of the programs; and ii) to identify the key factors of success, in order to strengthen the same programs and to guide the establishment of similar programs in other areas of the country. 
The monitoring and evaluation of the local program will have as elements: i) an emphasis on the laying down of projects (objectives, goals, activities, responsibilities, timetable) so that they can be evaluated; ii) the use of process indicators (costs, use of resources, productivity); and iii) a strict documentation of the experiences. On these bases, a periodic analysis of the impact of the actions being implemented will be done, having in mind the  objectives proposed under the responsibility of a multi-institutional and communal group permanently and autonomously in charge of monitoring each program. 
The evaluation of the experiences will be done annually, with the participation of the organisations behind the initiatives, the local agents and the community, and based on a guide prepared for each program. The participative emphasis will aim at identifying the strengths and weaknesses perceived by the community and, at the same time, it will try to make the analysis of the experiences in itself an instrument of collective learning and social cohesion. 
b. In the national context
The monitoring and evaluation of actions related to the laying down and execution of national policies aiming at the assistance to basic rights will have as objectives: i) the identification of the key factors of success of the national social programs, in terms of their conception, strategies, institutional management, allocation and use of resources, technology for the provision of resources and citizen participation; and ii) its use as an instrument for the accountability of the actions underway. 
As a consequence, they will have as their essential instruments: i) a strict laying down of the programs in terms of the expected objectives, activities, responsibilities, and deadlines; ii) an autonomous entity for the monitoring of processes and progress bein made;  and iii) advanced periodic reports known to the public. 
The monitoring of the national actions will be the responsibility of a specialised group to this effect, and made of the national organisms and agencies of cooperation participating.
c. In the international context
The monitoring and evaluation of actions in the international context will aim at the measurement of the effectivity of the adopted strategies, and at stimulating the reinforcement or reorientation of the promotional actions carried out by the Special Envoy or by the Resident Coordination System.
The monitoring will be carried out by an official of the Foreign Ministry, another one from the National Planning Department and by a representative of the United Nations System, who will lay down a monthly periodic advance report. At least quarterly, there will take place a meeting of evaluation and rectification of course, with the participation of the same three institutions.

Appendix 1:
Characteristics of the Human Development Observatory and Foreseen Indicators
Without information there is no accountability or public monitoring.
The transparency in the civil service, the development of a state under the rule of law and of democracy are based on the availability of opportune information.
The basis of public policies is the social pact (on the desirable objectives and the efforts necessary to reach them); and the basis and sustainability of the social pacts is information. 
Information on the economic and social situation must be of public knowledge for it to have a political character (as it happens in several countries where the inflation, unemployment, growth and education indicators are the basis of an evaluation of public administration).
Indicators do not change policies in themselves. Their availability must, therefore, go together with a broad spread and open debate on its implications. 
The main function of the technology of the systems of indicators is communication and the mobilisation of public opinion around compromises, goals and commitments, in order to orient public policies and to correct demonstrated imbalances.
General objective: to foster a mechanism of public monitoring of Human Development, that is, of the basic human rights situation  in Colombia, as a condition for accountability about the progress of the country in human development, and at the same time to make possible the public monitoring of the social and economic goals collectively adopted. 
Specific objectives: i) to facilitate the monitoring of human development in the country through the evaluation of recent results and the definition of objectives for the next period; ii) to contribute to the strengthening of democracy, the rule of law, the exercise of human rights and the development of human capital; iii) to promote the use of social information as a basic element of citizenship and to stimulate public monitoring of the public administration; iv) to stimulate decision making on the basis of information; and v) to be used as an instrument for the monitoring and evaluation of the results of the programs that count with the support of the United Nations System. 
Structure. The gathering, processing, refining and systematisation of information will be undertaken by national organisms with the support, whenever necessary, of the United Nations System. Public spread will be done monthly, quarterly and annually, as special reports of the United Nations System based on high-impact indicators. The annual report will include the progress made during the previous year, a proposal of feasible goals for the next year and thematic studies. For this, it is essential to establish an information service with a massive coverage, with a type of communication that warrants the prompt recognition by the public as points of comparison or as vital signs of the welfare of the population. Thus, information can become a political fact alluding to the worries of the public and its organisations, and stimulating it to take a stance on the monitoring of welfare and to have a bearing on the process of decisions on social and political programs. 
National and local monitoring. The Observatory will refer to the national context. There will also be local observatories in the departments and municipalities that decide to have them. 
In this manner, the United Nations System aspires to contribute to the strengthening of social cohesion and democracy in Colombia, to evaluate its own actions y to count on a solid basis for the orientation of the international community’s cooperation with the development of the country. 
The indicators have the following characteristics:
Understandable for the public in general.
In small quantities, to make the concentration of efforts easier. 
Related to essential  aspects of welfare and, therefore, related to the daily life of persons 
Opportune, with adequate periodicity and strict regularity
Sensible to changes in the situation in short periods
Technically reliable
Of public knowledge to make of information a political fact, and to make the monitoring by the public easier
As far as possible, information will be separated by gender and age
