1. Assumed International Obligations Regarding Human Rights
Colombia is signatory of most of the international treaties on human rights, of a world as well as a regional character.
However the country has not signed the Convention on the imprescriptibility of war crimes and of lese-humanity or the Interamerican Convention on forced disappearances. 
The Republic of Colombia has ratified the following instruments of the United Nations in the field of Human Rights:
International Pact of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
International Pact of Civil and Political Rights and its two additional protocols
Agreement on the Abolition of Forced Labour
Convention on Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading treatments.
International Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial Discrimination
International Convention on Repression and the Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid
Agreement Regarding Discrimination in matters of Employment and Occupation
Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women
Convention on the Political Rights of Women
Convention on the Rights of Children
International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of all Migrant Workers and their families
Convention on the Statute of Refugees and Protocol on the Statute of Refugees
Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide
Ottawa Agreement on the Elimination of Anti-personal Mines
It has also ratified the following treaties on International Humanitarian Law:
Geneva Agreement to relieve the fate of the wounded and sick of the armed forces when in campaign
Geneva Agreement to relieve the fate of the wounded, sick and shipwrecked of the armed forces in the sea (Agreement II) 
Geneva Agreement on the treatment given to prisoners of war (Agreement III)
Geneva Agreement regarding the protection due to civilians in time of war (Agreement IV)
Additional Protocol to the Geneva Agreements of August 12, 1949, regarding the protection of the victims of armed conflicts of an  international character (Protocol I)
Additional Protocol to the Geneva Agreements of August 12, 1949, regarding the protection of the victims of armed conflicts without an international character (Protocol II)
Reports of Instances created in virtue of the Treaties on Human Rights
The Human Rights Commission of the United Nations has dealt with Colombia for several years, specially since 1988, through its thematic procedures. Different thematic relators, representing the Secretary General, workgroups of the Human Rights Commission and human rights organisms created by the treaties, within the framework of their respective mandates, have examined specific cases or the global situation of human rights in Colombia.
During his first visit in October 1989 (E/CN. 1990/22/add.1), the Special Relator on Extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, had the opportunity to study exhaustively the Colombian situation regarding this matter, and as in most of his annual reports, denounced the cases of violations to the right to life, in great part committed by paramilitary groups against human rights defenders, labour leaders and civilians. He made a second visit in October, 1994, together with the Special Relator on Torture (E/CN.4/1995/111). 
On that occasion, both relators concluded that only if an effective fight against impunity takes place there will be an improvement in the exercise of human rights.  They consequently urge the government to fulfil its international obligation of making exhaustive investigations and compensating the victims or their families, and to adopt measures so that acts of that nature will no be repeated. They remark that the strengthening of ordinary justice is essential. They consider necessary that the government assign the necessary human and material resources, specially forensic physicians and ballistic experts. They also recommend special measures to protect members of the administration of justice and of the public prosecutors, as well as the witnesses. They point out that military justice should not look at cases of violation of human rights that should pass to ordinary justice. They suggest a substantial reform of the Military Penal Code and recommend the suspension from active service of members of the armed forces whenever the Office of the Public Prosecutor or the “Procuraduría” have opened against them disciplinary or penal investigations. They also favour, among many other recommendations, the dismantling of armed groups, specially of the paramilitary groups, and the taking of measures to fight against “social cleaning” aiming above all at street children. 
The Special Relator on the Independence and impartiality of Judges and Lawyers, was particularly concerned about the existence of “faceless courts” (already eliminated) and about the threats against defenders of human rights and lawyers. The Relator visited the country in September 1996 and layed down a report with recommendations on the legal system, most of which coincide with those put forward by other Relators (E/CN.4/1998/39/add.3).
The Special Relator on the Contemporary Manifestations of Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Connected Forms of Intolerance visited Colombia in 1996. He recommended in his report that a law on racial discrimination be adopted, that the process of assignation of lands to afrocolombian and indigenous communities be speeded, that these communities have a greater participation in the taking of decisions that affect them, and that they be protected against the violence generated by the armed conflict (E/CN.4/1997/71/add.1).
The representative of the Secretary General on Internal Displacement has in several occasions expressed his particular concern about the matter of internal displacement in Colombia. Colombia, in effect, is among the ten countries in the world with the greatest flow of forced displacement. The Representative has always favoured a significant presence of the international community in order to monitor the evolution of the phenomenon and to work jointly with the government and institutions in the search for solutions to the problem. The Representative visited Colombia for the first time in 1994 (E/CN.4/1995/50/ADD.1) In May 1999, the Representative visited Colombia for the second time, whose official conclusions are part of the agenda of the meeting of the Commission on Human Rights in March, 2000. 
The Work Group on Forced or Involuntary Disappearance, was one of the first to attend to the Colombian case (E/CN.4/1989/18/add.1) It has communicated its concern to the government about several cases of disappeared persons, attributed to the armed forces or to the security services. In the great majority of cases, the government has answered the requests reporting on the progress of the trials. The Work Group considers necessary the adoption of “legislative, administrative, judicial and other effective measures to prevent and stop acts of forced disappearance”. The Group stresses the fulfilment of the obligation to judge the presumed perpetrators of the disappearances in jurisdiction of special justice, specially the military one. They point at the necessity   of making habeas corpus a workable and effective instrument. 
The Work Group on Arbitrary Detention analysed several Colombian cases (E/CN.4/1995/31/Add.2) and has expressed the need for any exceptional measure to warrant the protection due to the magistrates who administer justice, must be compatible with international norms on the due process of law. 
The Committee on Human Rights, after studying the fourth periodic report presented by Colombia (CCPR/C/79/Add.75) acknowledged that the Colombian armed conflict had spread and that violations of human rights continued in massive form. The Committee issued several recommendations, among which the following stand out:
The need to investigate and sanction officers of the security services or of the armed forces implicated in the support for paramilitary groups;
the abolition of the law that created “Convivir”;
the adoption of strong measures to warrant the investigation of violations of human rights and compensation to the victims;
suspension of officers condemned for violations of human rights and of those on trial for violations of human rights, to be judged by independent civil courts, 
adoption of special measures of protection for defenders of human rights, labour leaders, political leaders, newspaper men, members of indigenous communities and judges;
reform of the Military Penal Code in conformity with international norms, in particular the exclusion clause of obedience to superiors;
training in human rights for the whole population, in particular for members of the armed forces, security officers, the police, judges, lawyers and professors;
revision of the legislation aiming to the attainment of the equality of women;
review of measures against violence;
fitting conditions of detention and adoption of alternative measures;
abolition of the system of regional justice;
respect to the due process of law;
measures to protect the life of minors, to avoid the conscription of children y to eliminate abusive employment of minors; 
adoption of measures to protect the rights of indigenous and afrocolombian communities.
The Committee for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination has studied the case of Colombia in several occasions. It has recommended that the government establish effective mechanisms to coordinate and evaluate the different policies for the protection of the rights of the indigenous and afrocolombian communities. These mechanisms must look after a real and adequate participation in public life of the representatives of these communities. It recommends that the state give the necessary assistance to the migratory processes, and to lay down programs of sensibilization to human rights and tolerance.
In its report (Supplement 44A/51/44), the Committee Against Torture pointed at the climate of widespread violence caused by the guerrillas, drug-trafficking and armed civil groups as obstacles to the implementation of the Convention. It recommended that the following measures be taken: the elimination of torture and the implantation of adequate sanctions, the elimination of armed civil and paramilitary groups, the adoption of legislative and administrative  measures for military courts to judge only the infractions against military regulations, the training of the armed forces and the police, and measures to favour compensation and the rehabilitation of victims. The Committee also suggests the fitting of the internal laws so as to fulfil the obligations of the Convention related to the no return or expulsion of those who fear torture, the extraterritorial and universal application of the law, the extradition or express nullity of proofs obtained under torture.
 The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women studied the case of Colombia in 1994 (Doc. A/50/38). On that occasion issued a series of recommendations: it suggested the inclusion of measures of affirmative action related to non sexist education and to the spread of the rights of women workers through the training of work inspectors in this area, the adoption of measures aiming at the elimination of violence against women, the modification of the legislation to reduce the number of abortions, the spread of programs of family planning in particular in rural areas, to promote the participation of women in the taking of decisions, and to reinforce the government mechanism responsible for the policies of equality, by assigning to it more human and financial resources. 
 In 1995 the Committee on the Pact of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights undertook the final study of the third periodic report presented by Colombia (Doc.E/C12/1995/12). The Committee went on record on the not so equitable distribution of wealth in Colombia and suggests that a solution be found for this problem by means of programs of economic development and a modification of the tax system. It recommends that the government give priority to the efforts to lighten the situation of indigenous communities, displaced persons, and persons living in the margin of society; a deep study of the fundamental causes of “social cleaning”; the adoption of measures tending to eradicate inequality between men and women; the adoption of the necessary measures to harmonise the legislation on labour liberty and collective bargaining; to guarantee the right to free primary education and to improve the quality of secondary education; to include the teaching on human rights in all levels of education, as well as in the training of policemen, members of the armed forces and  of the security services, magistrates and judges.
Related international obligations
Among the international agreements entered in by Colombia in areas related to the protection and exercise of human rights, arising from the General Assembly of the United States and of an obligatory character, the following stand out:
Laying down and implementing plans for the control of activities related to illicit drugs, eradication of illicit drugs, vigilance of precursors used in the manufacturing of drugs, intervention in the laundering of funds originated in drug-trafficking and application of the “Declaration of guiding principles for the reduction of the demand for drugs.”
